I think the fact that the government hasn't pointed to those suits is because, you know, you really do have to have the confluence of a claim that attaches to the permittee agency's decision-making that's not just a way to, you know, try another way of complaining about whatever it is the permitting agency, the permitting authority, does.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: If I could just make sure that your understanding of your own claim is that the final agency action here is the submission of the application. It's not any kind of preexisting decision or severable decision to go ahead with these operations that the Air Force has made. Or do you think that, in fact, there's no difference between the two?

turns.name: CAROLINE A. FLYNN
turns.text: I think there's no difference between the two, and that's why I'm fully comfortable with saying that the final agency action is the submission of the application. I think the application reflects the decision. It's memorialized there. And it also implements it by bringing about the automatic extension but also by binding Air Force personnel to the application's terms upon Guam EPA's approval.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: And I guess the question is: It reflects the decision to do what? Mr. Joshi says, from the very beginning, it reflects the decision to make a proposal to another agency that has the authority to say yes or no, et cetera, et cetera. And you said that has no bearing on whether or not we should consider this final agency action?

turns.name: CAROLINE A. FLYNN
turns.text: I think it --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: I mean, you do agree that it's -- it's the decision to make a proposal?

turns.name: CAROLINE A. FLYNN
turns.text: May I --

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Yes, of course.

turns.name: CAROLINE A. FLYNN
turns.text: I think it reflects the decision to continue these operations past when they otherwise would have ceased because the Air Force was forced to a choice: Do we want to stop when our permit would expire, or do we want to keep going? And I think it reflects the decision to keep going. And I think that is fully the Air Force's decision to make. That's not Guam EPA's decision to make. And, yes, it leads to teeing up this other decision by the regulator, but that doesn't change the Air Force made its own decision.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, counsel. Oh, Justice Thomas?

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: I'd like to go back to my point. When we had the Seven County case here, the Surface Transportation Board considered the proposal of Seven County to build the railroad spur, and it was the Surface Transportation Board's NEPA report that was being considered. Here, we -- you're saying that the regulated body -- and, of course, there was a final agency action there because they actually submitted that. But, here, you're saying that the regulated body that submits the proposal actually has engaged in and -- a -- a -- a final agency action. And I asked you for any other examples that you might have of the regulated body's request or application being considered a final agency action.

turns.name: CAROLINE A. FLYNN
turns.text: So no other example comes to mind in this Court's case law, but I would say that it's clear that NEPA attaches to the -- to federal agencies' own operations, so their actions about, you know, like the operations here, what they are doing and not just their actions as a regulator. And so I think the upshot of --

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: No, we're -- we're not -- excuse me. I'm sorry. I'm sorry to interrupt you. We're not talking about the NEPA requirement. We're talking about whether or not the APA final agency action applies for the purpose of using APA as an avenue to challenging this.

turns.name: CAROLINE A. FLYNN
turns.text: Right. And I was -- what I was getting at is that if it were true that there can never be final agency action when the government's own operations are involved and they're not acting as a regulator, you would never be able to bring an action challenging a NEPA violation for the government's own operations, even though that seems like, you know --

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: That's --

turns.name: CAROLINE A. FLYNN
turns.text: -- a pretty clear --

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: -- that's -- that's not the point I'm making. It's -- I'm -- the point I'm making is, is there final agency action when the government is the applicant, not whether or not it's taking an action?

turns.name: CAROLINE A. FLYNN
turns.text: Yes. Our position is that there is because they reached the culmination of their decision-making process about their own operations but about the decision at hand and it produced legal consequences.

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: Do you have another example of that happening?

turns.name: CAROLINE A. FLYNN
turns.text: I would say Biden versus Texas, the agency was deciding its own policy for immigration enforcement. So the DHS Secretary was making a decision about what DHS employees would do. That's what this Court framed it as, was a determination of what DHS employees would have to do once the injunction in that case -- or if the injunction in that case was lifted. So I do think this Court's finality inquiry is no different when it comes to the federal government's actions, you know, as an entity carrying out its own operations and not just its actions as a regulator.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Alito? Justice Sotomayor? Justice Kagan? Justice Gorsuch?

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: I guess I'm just a little curious. Do you think you could bring -- I'm repeating myself for both of you. Do you think you could bring an action for agency action unlawfully withheld, and why -- why didn't you try that avenue?

turns.name: CAROLINE A. FLYNN
turns.text: With apologies, I -- that's not the action we brought here, and I don't want to make commitments about a question when it arose in a different case.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Okay. All right. Thank you.

turns.name: CAROLINE A. FLYNN
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Kavanaugh? Justice Barrett?

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: No.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Jackson? No? Thank you, counsel. Rebuttal, Mr. Joshi.

turns.name: SOPAN JOSHI
turns.text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice. Just a few points. First, to address the questions that Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kavanaugh had, our position, just to be clear, is that the claim, as we understand it, and I think Ms. Flynn confirmed, was that they are saying the submission of the RCRA application is final agency action. We don't think that's final agency action. And, indeed, the submission of the application, our position is, that that is just not agency action at all. It'll never become final. It's just an application. The final permit, when it issues, will be final, but it'll be final from the regulating entity, Guam EPA, or federal EPA if it's Iowa. As far as when the Air Force's action becomes final, I mean, if it's a case where, as Justice Thomas was suggesting, if after receiving a permit the agency issued an order saying, now go blow up these waste munitions on Guam, that would be an order. That would be a final agency action. If Respondent wants to bring a claim saying, even absent such an order, there is a silent, implicit order, we can have that fight. We'd probably oppose that. I'm sure they would say, no, there really is an order, and that would be a final agency action. But that would have nothing to do with the RCRA permit. It would have nothing to do with the RCRA permit application, which is what we're concerned with here. And that gets me to my second point, which is Ms. Flynn said she wasn't worried about opening the floodgates. I don't see how. If you find that submission of a RCRA permit application is final agency action because the applicant happens to be a federal agency, I don't know how you distinguish it from any one of the tens of thousands of permit applications that federal agencies file and hold at the current time. Every single application would be final action, which could immediately trigger a lawsuit. And it doesn't have to be a procedural lawsuit, as Ms. Flynn said. It could be anything. It could be your application was arbitrary and capricious because you didn't consider X, Y, and Z. You shouldn't have applied for it. You should have decided to do something different. And if the application is revised, you're going to have another lawsuit, three years of litigation in between. And then, when the final permit issues, I suppose we'll have yet another one. So I think the floodgates are real. And, yes, Ms. Flynn is right that once there is some final action, a permit is issued, if the agency issues an order and does something, there will be a lawsuit then. That's unavoidable in our system. But the whole point of the finality rule is to challenge all of the challenges into a single proceeding at the end. Finally, I just want to say, in terms of, Justice Alito, you were asking about conflict and impossibility and when do both statutes apply, I don't think it's right that there has to be a metaphysical impossibility of complying with both statutes. I think a conflict can be just inconsistency between the two, with a specific and a general. And, again, the best case for that I think I'd cite is an environmental case. It's Home Builders, which we cite in our brief. And that was one where the Clean Water Act had, I think, nine criteria that EPA had to look at and see if they were satisfied, and the claim that the plaintiffs brought there was: Well, by its terms, the Endangered Species Act could also apply to this situation. And the Court said we are not going to engraft additional requirements. Given how reticulated the Clean Water Act is with nine requirements, we're not going to engraft a tenth. I think the same would be true here. Unless the Court has further questions, we'd ask to reverse.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, counsel. The case is submitted.
